connection_type: I have direct personal experience (as an immigrant, refugee, religious minority, or member of a marginalised group)
disclosure_text: I moved to a new area last year. Because of this, I have personal experience with adjusting to a new community, dealing with a different culture, and trying to find a sense of belonging in a new place.
micronarrative:
I grew up in a small town where people kept to themselves and focused on their own lives. This environment taught me early on that it’s best to mind my own business and not get involved in other people’s personal disagreements unless it directly affects me. When my two close friends started arguing and both tried to draw me into their dispute, it felt like walking past a crowd of people in the street. I could see the tension, but I didn’t want to force myself to take a side or feel forced to do so.

I remember the discomfort of having to listen to both sides of the story, each friend presenting their version with conviction. It was like being caught in the middle of a storm, but I couldn’t help but feel the weight of their expectations. I knew I had to find a way to navigate this without compromising my own values or relationships.

I decided to listen more and speak less, focusing on expressing my care for both friends while maintaining my neutrality. I told them, “I care about you both, but I want to keep our conversations separate from this disagreement because of how much I value our friendship.” This approach allowed me to set clear boundaries without offending anyone. It was a delicate dance, but one that helped me stay true to myself and maintain my friendships.
